items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: Wally Alpren, who went on to become a federal judge, was guitar player.

ctx.x: Well it was all standard stuff, it was all 32-bar tunes, it was all that. And harmonic structure you could figure out pretty much the chord changes and the chord changes were all pretty simple. And you could learn to play well enough to do it. And so the consequence was that all over the Northeast you had these amateur college Dixieland bands. Everywhere. The Crimson Stompers at Harvard, Tigertown Five at Princeton, Eli’s Chosen Six at Yale. You had a band at Amherst, you had a band at Williams, you had Hamilton,…

know. We thought we were playing the blues, God knows it was terrible. But then I began to meet guys around the campus who were interested in jazz because you’d be drawn together with people like that just by chance and by the next year we had a little band: Mike Beldock on drums — Mike went on to be an important defense attorney. He was the one who got Hurricane Carter out of jail — Myron Beldock. And his partner, Elliot Abrams is a big music lawyer — not Elliot Abrams, Elliot Hoffman was a big music lawyer who…
It was a lot of fun I’ll bet.
